title: Burst SLO Simulation and Cost Sampling Methodology
author: Priya Nair
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines the canonical methodology we use for simulating short-duration (burst) traffic patterns to validate latency SLOs and surface per-token cost amplification effects in the runtime. It combines a workload model, kernel-scheduler assumptions, KV cache warmup dynamics, and a cost-sampling strategy so experiment results are comparable across teams and releases.

Goals
-----
- Provide a repeatable experimental recipe for measuring impact of bursts on P50/P95/P99 latency and per-token cost.
- Quantify cost amplification (extra GPU cycles or tokens) caused by cold KV caches, scheduling preemption, and cross-tenant contention.
- Produce sampling guidance so cost estimates converge within 5% for 95% of runs.
- Tie results to clear operational mitigations (routing, cache warming, priority shaping).

Scope and Non-Goals
-------------------
- In scope: latency SLO regressions from 10s–30s bursts, KV cache cold-warm transitions, kernel scheduling backpressure, and short-window autoscaling behavior.
- Out of scope: long-term capacity planning (multi-hour), per-customer billing reconciliation, and model-quality degradation.

Key concepts and assumptions
----------------------------
- Burst window: contiguous arrival period where QPS > baseline by >= 3x for at least 10s. Default burst window used in experiments: 15s and 60s.
- Cost amplification: ratio of observed GPU token-cost (compute + memory overhead) to steady-state per-token cost. Expressed as a multiplier (e.g., 1.45x).
- KV cache hit-rate curve: we model cache warming as an exponential rise: hit(t) = H_inf * (1 - exp(-t / tau)), where tau is warmup time constant (default 8s for a single shard).
- Kernel preemption latency: scheduling pause introduced when a higher-priority request preempts a kernel. Default preemption penalty: 1.8 ms per preemption event on Ampere A100 80GB nodes (profiled).

Workload model
--------------
1) Arrival process
   - Poisson baseline with lambda_b (e.g., 50 qps). Bursts are injected by superimposing a short-duration spike modeled as a log-normal multiplicative factor.
   - Configurable burst shapes: square (instant increase), ramp (linear increase over 2–5s), and fat-tail (pareto-distributed dense tail).
2) Sequence length distribution
   - Empirical histograms from production: short (<= 64 tokens) — 60%, mid (65–512) — 30%, long (>512) — 10%.
   - For burst sensitivity tests use parameterized scale-up factors for long sequences.
3) Prefix reuse / KV locality
   - Hot prefixes: small set of user prefixes that account for high fraction of tokens. We simulate hot-prefix ratio H_frac ∈ {0.05, 0.15, 0.30}.

Kernel scheduling and resource model
----------------------------------
- Scheduler abstraction used by the simulation mirrors primary runtime decisions: continuous batching (CB), preemptive priority shepherding (PPS), and kernel crediting. Each simulated request consumes a schedule quantum proportional to tokens x compute_profile.
- Priority classes modeled: latency-critical, standard, background. Preemption rules: latency-critical can steal up to 30% of kernel credits; standard requests are throttled when queue depth > Q_thresh (default 120).
- GPU resource model includes occupancy and tensor-core efficiency drop when active concurrent SMs < 60% (empirical). We model efficiency as a step curve to reflect kernel-size sensitivity.

KV cache behavior in simulation
------------------------------
- Sharded KV cache model: N_shards (typ. 4) with consistent-hash mapping. We simulate shard-skew by drawing per-shard traffic from a Dirichlet distribution (alpha configurable).
- Eviction policy: LRU with small protected window to approximate prefix pinning.
- Cache warming: requests routed to cold shards incur a KV fetch penalty (default +6ms) and increase backend I/O.

Metrics and instrumentation (what to collect)
--------------------------------------------
Collect the following per-experiment and report aggregated stats. All metrics below are defined at token granularity unless noted.

- latency.p50/p95/p99.request-ms (per request)
- tokens.total and tokens.served_from_kvcache
- kvcache.hit_rate (per-shard and global)
- kernel.preemptions.count and kernel.preemptions.mean_delay_ms
- gpu_utilization.percent (time-weighted)
- per_token_compute_cycles and per_token_memory_bytes (aggregated)
- cost.estimated_usd (simulation-calculated using current cost model)
- amplification.factor = cost.estimated_usd / steady_state_cost

Sampling strategy for cost estimation
------------------------------------
Goal: keep variance low while bounding experiment time. Use a hybrid stratified + reservoir approach:
1) Stratify by sequence-length bucket and hot-prefix membership (two strata).
2) For each stratum, use reservoir sampling with target sample sizes that ensure 95% CI width <= 5% for per-stratum mean cost. Default targets: short: 4000 samples, mid: 2000, long: 800.
3) If experiment time is constrained, prioritize long-sequence samples (they dominate cost variance) using adaptive reallocation.

Experiment configuration (canonical table)
-----------------------------------------
| name                        | default | description |
|-----------------------------|---------|-------------|
| baseline_qps                | 50      | steady-state QPS before burst |
| burst_multiplier            | 6       | peak/steady ratio |
| burst_duration_s            | 15      | primary short-window test |
| burst_shape                 | square  | square | ramp | fat-tail |
| kvcache_shards              | 4       | number of logical KV shards |
| kvcache_skew_alpha          | 0.6     | Dirichlet alpha for shard skew (lower = more skewed) |
| preemption_penalty_ms      | 1.8     | scheduler preemption penalty per event |
| sample_targets              | short=4000,mid=2000,long=800 | per-stratum reservoir target |

CLI and config examples
-----------------------
- Example experiment yaml (experiment.yaml):

```yaml
experiment_name: burst-slo-validation-2025-03
baseline_qps: 50
burst:
  multiplier: 6
  duration_s: 15
  shape: square
sequence_distribution:
  short: 0.6
  mid: 0.3
  long: 0.1
kvcache:
  shards: 4
  skew_alpha: 0.6
scheduler:
  preemption_penalty_ms: 1.8
sampling:
  targets:
    short: 4000
    mid: 2000
    long: 800
```

- Run command (cluster test harness):

$ ri-sim run --config experiment.yaml --out results/burst-2025-03-18.tar.gz --seed 42

Interpreting results and pass/fail criteria
------------------------------------------
1) Latency SLOs
   - Primary: P95 <= 120 ms, P99 <= 400 ms for latency-critical class during burst window.
   - Secondary: Average P95 across standard class should degrade < 1.5x from baseline.
2) Cost amplification
   - Pass if amplification.factor <= 1.25 for 15s bursts and <= 1.45 for 60s bursts under H_frac <= 0.15.
3) Operational readiness
   - If preemption rate > 0.7 events/sec per GPU or kvcache.global_hit_rate < 0.6 then fail and follow remediation runbook.

Common failure modes and mitigations (runbook)
--------------------------------------------
- Symptom: High P99 with low KV hit rate\  Causes: shard skew or cold restart\  Immediate actions: 1) Pin hot prefixes or increase protected window; 2) Temporarily route hot prefixes to warmed dedicated shard pool; 3) Trigger background cache-warm job (see runbook steps).
- Symptom: High cost amplification but stable latency\  Causes: excessive background rebuilds or inefficient kernel paths\  Actions: 1) Collect kernel flamegraphs; 2) Enable conservative batching to reduce repeated kernel launches; 3) Adjust quantization profile for high variance token widths.
- Symptom: Frequent preemptions causing jitter\  Causes: aggressive priority stealing from latency-critical pool\  Actions: 1) Lower preemptive cap from 30% to 15% for affected nodes; 2) Use priority routing to spread latency-critical across additional GPU capacity; 3) Temporarily increase queue depth thresholds to allow batching to complete.

Detailed remediation procedure: cache-warm job
----------------------------------------------
1) Identify hot-prefix list from telemetry (kvcache.top_k_prefixes, window=5m).
2) Prepare warm job config: include prefix list and target shard mapping. Example: ri-kv-warm --input prefixes.txt --concurrency 8 --target-shards 4.
3) Schedule on non-production-backed warmers or during low-util windows.
4) Post-warm verification: kvcache.hit_rate per-shard should increase by >= 0.25 within 90s.

Release tracking and experiment reproducibility
---------------------------------------------
- Each experiment must be linked to a runtime-release tag (git commit) and a kernel artifact version. Store experiment.yaml, seed, and the full result tarball in the artifacts bucket under path: s3://redwood-bench-results/{release}/{experiment_name}/{timestamp}/.
- Example metadata record to attach to results (CSV-friendly fields only): release_tag, git_sha, kernel_version, seed, config_sha256, runtime_image, notes.

Known limitations and open questions
----------------------------------
- Simulation abstracts network jitter and RPC fanout; we recommend correlating with a small on-cluster canary for every major change.
- Cost model sensitivity to GPU spot pricing is not captured. Separate sensitivity sweep is required for billing impact.
- Multi-tenant cross-customer interference is modeled only via synthetic priority classes; we lack a labeled corpus of production cross-tenant interference events.

---------------------------------------------

Appendix B — Quick checklist before labeling release
---------------------------------------------------
- Run canonical 15s and 60s burst experiments for all supported instance types.
- Confirm cost amplification <= threshold and kernel preemptions within limits.
- Upload artifacts and attach experiment metadata to release ticket.
